chunks.text: Rameez Khan is a Software Engineer. Software engineer. Second brain. Building things that matter.

Rameez Khan is a software engineer who writes about data engineering, Go, SQL, and developer tooling. His technical writing covers SQL window functions in BigQuery (FIRST_VALUE and LAST_VALUE frame clause behaviour), dbt unit testing for macros using dbt 1.8 native unit tests, Goose database schema migration tool for Go services, and Go error handling patterns including sentinel errors, error wrapping with fmt.Errorf, and custom error types. His projects include ox-db (a TypeScript database query tool with a clean UI for writing and executing SQL across multiple database types) and bragdoc (a second brain tool for tracking professional accomplishments — designed for performance reviews, interviews, and 1:1s). He has a machine learning background including a self-driving car project using CNNs and behavioral cloning. He is active on GitHub as rxmeez and publishes on Medium as @rxmeez. His interests span backend systems, data pipelines, and tools that make developers more effective.

chunks.source: Untangling FIRST_VALUE and LAST_VALUE in BigQuery SQL
chunks.text: Window functions in SQL are powerful — until they're not. FIRST_VALUE and LAST_VALUE are two functions that seem straightforward but often produce unexpected results when you don't fully understand their frame clause behavior. The Problem Consider this common pattern: you want the first and last value within a partition. You write: SELECT category, sale_date, amount, FIRST_VALUE(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY category ORDER BY sale_date) AS first_sale, LAST_VALUE(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY category ORDER BY sale_date) AS last_sale FROM sales ORDER BY category, sale_date; You might expect LAST_VALUE to give you the last row in the partition.

chunks.source: Untangling FIRST_VALUE and LAST_VALUE in BigQuery SQL
chunks.text: It doesn't — unless you specify the window frame correctly. The Fix: Explicit Frame Clauses The default frame for LAST_VALUE is RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW . This means it only looks from the start to the current row — effectively returning the current row's value, not the partition's last value.

chunks.source: Untangling FIRST_VALUE and LAST_VALUE in BigQuery SQL
chunks.text: LAST_VALUE(amount) OVER ( PARTITION BY category ORDER BY sale_date ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING ) AS last_sale Key Takeaways Always specify the window frame explicitly when using LAST_VALUE FIRST_VALUE works as expected with the default frame because it starts from UNBOUNDED PRECEDING Consider using ARRAY_AGG with ORDER BY and LIMIT 1 as an alternative pattern in BigQuery This is a common pitfall that catches even experienced SQL developers. The key is understanding that window functions don't "see" the entire partition by default — they see a sliding window defined by the frame clause. Read the full article on Medium ↗

chunks.source: DBT Unit Tests: Expanding to Macros
chunks.text: dbt 1.8 introduced native unit testing — a feature the community has been asking for. While most of the documentation focuses on testing models, there's a powerful use case that deserves more attention: unit testing macros. Why Test Macros? Macros are the backbone of reusable logic in dbt. A broken macro can silently corrupt data across dozens of models. Unit tests give you confidence that your Jinja logic is correct before it touches real data.

chunks.source: DBT Unit Tests: Expanding to Macros
chunks.text: A Practical Example Here's a macro that normalizes email addresses: {% macro normalize_email(email_column) %} LOWER(TRIM({{ email_column }})) {% endmacro %} And the unit test: unit_tests: - name: test_normalize_email model: stg_users given: - input: ref('stg_users') rows: - {email: ' User@Example.COM '} expect: rows: - {email: 'user@example.com'} Key Patterns Test edge cases: nulls, empty strings, special characters Test macros in isolation before testing models that use them Use given fixtures to mock input data precisely Version your test fixtures alongside your macro code Unit testing macros catches logic errors early and makes refactoring safe.

chunks.source: DBT Unit Tests: Expanding to Macros
chunks.text: If you're on dbt 1.8+, start with your most critical macros — the ones that touch the most models. Read the full article on Towards Dev ↗

Database migrations are one of those things every project needs but nobody wants to think about. Goose is a minimal, no-fuss migration tool written in Go that deserves more attention. Why Goose Over Alternatives? Unlike ORM-coupled migration tools, Goose works with plain SQL files. You write .sql files, and Goose applies them in order. No DSL, no framework lock-in.

Getting Started go install github.com/pressly/goose/v3/cmd/goose@latest goose -dir migrations create add_users_table sql This creates two files: -- 20240527000000_add_users_table.up.sql CREATE TABLE users ( id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY, email TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE, created_at TIMESTAMPTZ DEFAULT now() ); -- 20240527000000_add_users_table.down.sql DROP TABLE users; Key Features Embedded migrations: Use Go's embed package to bundle migrations into your binary Transaction safety: Each migration runs in a transaction by default Multi-database: PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite, SQL Server, and more Go-based migrations: For complex logic, write migrations in Go instead of SQL If you're building a Go application that needs database migrations, Goose is worth a look.
It's battle-tested, actively maintained, and stays out of your way. Read the full article on Medium ↗

Go's error handling is one of its most debated features. No exceptions, no try-catch — just values. But once you understand the philosophy, it becomes one of Go's greatest strengths. Errors Are Values In Go, errors are just values that implement the error interface: type error interface { Error() string } This simplicity means you can treat errors like any other value: wrap them, chain them, inspect them. Common Patterns Sentinel Errors var ErrNotFound = errors.New("not found") func FindUser(id string) (*User, error) { // ...

return nil, ErrNotFound } // Caller checks: if errors.Is(err, ErrNotFound) { // handle not found } Error Wrapping (Go 1.13+) func GetConfig() (*Config, error) { data, err := os.ReadFile("config.json") if err != nil { return nil, fmt.Errorf("reading config: %w", err) } // parse...

} Custom Error Types type ValidationError struct { Field string Value interface{} } func (e *ValidationError) Error() string { return fmt.Sprintf("invalid %s: %v", e.Field, e.Value) } Best Practices Handle errors at the level where you have context to decide what to do Wrap errors with fmt.Errorf("%w", err) to preserve the original Use errors.Is and errors.As for type-safe error inspection Don't log and return — pick one Reserve panics for truly unrecoverable situations Go's explicit error handling forces you to think about failure modes at every step. That's not a bug — it's the feature. Read the full article on Medium ↗

Goose is a Go migration tool that uses plain SQL. No ORM lock-in, no DSL. Install & Create go install github.com/pressly/goose/v3/cmd/goose@latest goose -dir migrations create add_users_table sql Key Patterns Each migration gets .up.sql and .down.sql files Runs in transactions by default Supports embedding migrations into Go binaries Multi-database: PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite, SQL Server I use Goose for all Go services. Plain SQL + version control beats ORM magic.
